I've seen some claims that the gas is stored at a pressure of 10000 psi/690 bar in a 200 l tank. If that's true, then that is a gas volume of 138000 l. A commercial, stationary scuba compressor compresses around 850 l/min [0] to 350 bar. A compressor like that would take around 160 min just to compress 138000 l to 350 bar (so significantly less than 690 bar), is a _large_ appliance, and _loud_. Compressing gas quickly also produces heat. An on-board compressor seems quite unrealistic to me unless I'm missing something.

> Dermatologists are hit or miss.

That's even relative to the condition you have. The right match of doctor to condition gives you the right treatment. But the same doctor facing a different condition might be clueless. From that angle, the whole situation looks less weird.

The quality of a doctor then could be measured in how many conditions they are good at, maybe weighted by likelihood of occurrence, as well as how self aware they are about whether they have a clue or not.

A corrollary is that a single data point does not tell you much. "Go to this dermatologist, they are great" is only good advice if you have the same condition as the recommender as their sample size is likely very small.

They probably meant things like LLVM and the various optimization passes. None of those are verified, there’s probably all sorts of correctness issues, and yet it’s still ok. Rust’s usage also has issues and bugs emitting the right intermediate form for LLVM to consume and usually also it’s ok.

Would it be nice if we had even higher level of quality? Yes. But what’s neat is we have empirical evidence - Rust code does achieve the memory safety goals over C++ even though there’s bugs in the compiler. That’s why Rust is very quickly eating all things C and C++. A huge amount of value that the industry would just be unable to access for a long time if you waited for everything to be formally proven.

I usually listen to what doctors have to say, and trust their judgment. Especially since I have next to no formal education in bio or medicine.

I did resort to "self-diagnosis" once, though: for R-CPD (no-burp syndrome). Most doctors simply don't know this condition exists. I brought it up with my GP (whose referral I needed to see a specialist in Ontario), prepared for some pushback, but was pleasantly surprised that he did some brief research and then helped me forward.

Then again, I may have been lucky. I still hear stories of doctors who are less than cooperative when patients bring them "self-diagnoses", even for something as open-and-shut as R-CPD. But if most of those "diagnoses" are BS, then I can empathize with the docs, too.
